title: The Covering of Shame and the Poverty of Sin
english: They were in all evil; they did not have a garment covering the reasoning faculty, and the word was not being hidden by irrational passions. But when sin has happened, both the remaining feeling, thought, and life, and shame have increased.

If therefore we approach the light, by which we ceased sinning, our faces are not being shamed, and we have much boldness; for he says: 'if our heart does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God' (1 John 3:20). If someone sees himself as uncondemned by heart and conscience, he has much boldness toward God, as to say: 'the Lord lives, to whom I stood before him'. Having spoken with boldness: 'in the morning I will stand before you and I will watch; I will see many things, but even more I will observe; I will observe things to be seen'. 'And your faces will by no means be shamed' (Psalm 5:12).

We say that when sin exists, the face of the soul is covered by shame so that its beauty and the proportion of its melodies can no longer be seen. But when illumination comes, the remaining 'with an unveiled face, the glory of the Lord is reflected' (2 Cor 3:18). No one having a covered face reflects the glory of God, but rather if someone has cast off the coverings that came upon him. Those, indeed, having received perception, that evils have become by themselves, say: 'dishonor has covered our face'. Dishonor has become a covering for us, the shame, of our face.

7 This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him (Psalm 34:6). 117 They show someone to be poor by being in sin, poor in all evil. If someone, having become without evil, having cast off the wealth of ignorance, cries to God from this evil, he has Him listening. Perhaps, as they implied locally regarding the time, that which belongs to the lesser and the greater, encouraging those already illuminated and blessing 'the Lord at all times' (Psalm 34:8) to be rich, he says: and if the poor man approaches and cries, he is heard.

And it is possible also to say this concerning the people from among the Gentiles, that: the people 'not having hope and being godless in the world' (1 Thess 4:17) approached and cried and had Him listening to them. For he says with other things in the same psalm: 'the rich have become poor and hungered' (Psalm 39:7), saying those from the circumcision have become poor by having cast away the law and the prophets. Because of this, he also says pointedly: 'this poor man'; worthy.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nourishment of the Inner Man
english: Is it against [the law]? Observe: one angel, at the will of God, struck down one hundred eighty-five thousand in a single blow (Ps 78:49), and perhaps he was not a pure angel, since he was not acting to punish. Therefore, the perfect man who guards holiness, being God's own eyewitness and servant, is able to save many who fear Him.

If the explanation seems violent to anyone, not so: just as it is said, 'God made man' (Gen 1:26), to be the ruler of irrational animals, and we are not speaking of the individual kind, nor of this specific one, but the whole species. 'I made earth and man upon it' (Gen 1:1); thus he named the whole species. Even so, the angel here may signify the general, that those fearing the Lord have angels intervening and surrounding them, saving them from every tribulation.

You have this in the Gospel: 'See that you do not cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble; for their angels always see the face of our Father in heaven' (Matt 18:10). They stand before God, we see His face, they see the invisible one invisibly. Behold, therefore, of the many little ones, many angels are spoken of, but of those fearing the Lord, one angel is said. It is said singularly, for not even one [is excluded].

And this can also be said: the little ones do not fear God, but have a passive fear; for 'perfect love casts out fear' (1 John 4:18). And: 'fear has punishment'. 'Do not fear those who kill the body but are not able to kill the soul' (Matt 10:28); but those who fear God have an excessive fear, about which it is said in Sirach: 'the fear of the Lord surpassed all things' (Sir 1:14), which comes to him who seeks Him with much progress.

Therefore, these who fear the Lord can have one angel intervening and saving them, the Savior himself, about whom it is said: 'His name is called Angel of Great Counsel' (Isa 9:6); for in many writings an angel is mentioned not applying to any single person. Jacob also says of him: 'the angel who saves me from all evils' (Gen 48:16). But no one is able to save from all evils except the Savior who has the authority to forgive all sin. And of the sin...

Once the punishment is assigned, the following afflictions follow, joining together with that evil. It is like a perimeter and a wall surrounding them, keeping them safe from harm. And in Zechariah, namely the eleventh of the twelve prophets, it says: 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited desolately' (Zech 8:10), and it says: 'And I will be around them like a pillar of fire and a wall encircling them' (Zech 2:5). But it is fire for the purpose of harming those approaching more; for immediately in that same region of the prophet it says: 'because he who touches you touches the apple of his eye' (Zech 2:8). To touch there means to harm, like: 'Touch not my anointed ones' (Ps 105:15). Taste and see that the Lord is good (Ps 34:8).

Many times it has been said to us that the sensible and bodily things are like this: each thing is only what it is; for example, a stream is nothing other than a stream, or bread. But the thing that nourishes the inner man is called food according to various thoughts. It is indeed called light, it is called a spring, it is called bread and flesh, true nourishment. It says, therefore, 'taste' by the incorporeal taste of the inner man, 'and see that the Lord is good' (Ps 34:8), because He is good. Just taste, know that He is nourishment, see the spring of goodness, the spring of kindness.

Blessed is the man who hopes in Him (Ps 1:1). The one hoping in the good Lord—for he tastes Him—and he will experience His sweetness, and from this food he will have all things, and being nourished athletically he will be strong, so that in the struggle he no longer has it 'not toward blood and flesh, but toward principalities and powers' (Eph 6:12). 'Taste and see that He is good' (Ps 34:8). If anyone is weary and sick according to the soul, let him taste Him as nourishment, as one preparing health, as one removing harm. And this food not only satisfies, but also removes, casting out the harmful things.

Therefore, 'blessed' is not simply the man, but the 'man' who has done away with 'the things of a child' (1 Cor 13:11), who has not walked 'in the counsel of the ungodly' (Ps 1:1), nor sat 'in the seat of scoffers' (Ps 1:1), nor 'in the way of sinners' (Ps 1:1), nor 'on the seat of scoffers' (Ps 1:1), but having 'his will in the law of the Lord' (Ps 1:2). This one has his will in the law of the Lord; for many observe the law so that they may not be punished or so that they may be honored with praise. But the holy one, the...

title: The Poverty of the Rich and the Fullness of Seekers
english: A perfect man has his own will within the law of the Lord, in such a way that his will is not something different from the legal will. And this legal will is this: to forbid evil and to protect virtue. Therefore, when someone becomes a law to himself—for 'these are to themselves a law, not having a law' (Rom 2:29)—it is as if he has his own law intertwined with the law of the Lord. 'Fear the Lord, all his saints' (Ps 112:7), for there is no lack for those fearing him. I urge all the saints to fear him, the Lord. It has been said in Isaiah: 'He himself shall be your fear' (Isa 33:15). Let him himself become your fear. And just as food becomes nourishment to some, and wisdom makes others wise, and righteousness makes others righteous, so they also partake of sanctification; for he himself is also the sanctification, 'who became to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption' (1 Cor 1:30). Therefore, 'fear the Lord, all his saints.' His saints; for they are not merely called holy in a simple sense, but not [necessarily] his. As many as are being shaped into holiness seem to be saints, but not of God. And he gives the reason why 'all'; for 'there is no lack for those fearing him.' The fear of God makes [them] unshakable and unabandoned. 'Fear the Lord, all his saints.' Since 'there is no lack for those fearing him,' in order that you might become unabandoned, fear him, the God. And the fear of God is not passive, as I have said, but equal to reverence, equal to piety. When we take up a conception of God, fear immediately increases and piety arises; for we do not fear him as if we were terrified of him, not as if he were some bogeyman, but as something supremely venerable. And since the holy church stands glorious at the right hand of the Savior, all those completing it are saints. Therefore, concerning the calling of the Gentiles, it can be said: 'Fear the Lord, all his saints,' for there is no lack for those fearing him. 'The rich have fallen away and are hungry, but those seeking the Lord shall not lack any good thing' (Ps 34:10). The former, those completing the assembly before the arrival, [were] rich...

Being rich, they fell into poverty. The rich became impoverished and hungered, but those seeking the Lord shall not be diminished from every good thing. When the kingdom of God was taken from them, when the understanding of the divine writings departed from them, when they turned away from the old writing and from themselves, they became poor from being rich; for indeed this wealth fully benefits the possessor—for it becomes for him both food, and a covering, and a garment—so he says that these rich ones, having become poor, hungered. They cast away the spiritual food, they turned away from the 'bread of life'. They became poor; yet even if they themselves became poor, those seeking the Lord are not diminished from the good things, but they become full of them, they shall partake of them perfectly; for just as the kingdom of the heavens was taken from them—this also the mother of Jesus says: 'He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty' (Luke 1:53).

Those formerly rich were sent away empty; for even if they possess the books of Moses and the prophets, they are empty of their divine fullness. Fullness, therefore, of the divine writing is not the shadow, but the truth and the Spirit. 'Those seeking' therefore 'the Lord'—the seeking implies a longing—are filled with all good things. Concerning this also the singer says, conversing with his own soul: 'Bless the Lord, O my soul, who fills your desire with good things' (Psalm 103:2). And: 'Trust in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart' (Psalm 37:4).

Upon it, those passing from the shadow of the law and from partial knowledge and prophecy, find all things good. But primarily the spiritual things of the law are good, unceasing and most full; for these lead one toward the truth face to face, that which brings the perfection, in which no one shall be imperfect. 12 Come, children, listen to me. I will teach you the fear of the Lord calmly, concerning the necessity of taking up fear toward God, and how some, having fallen away from him, have become poor and needy from being rich, and that those seeking the Lord whom they fear, are filled with all good things; therefore, toward all those becoming his children, he composes the teaching, saying: 'Come, children, listen'.
